newsitem.title: GERMANY: German churches call for asylum law reform.
newsitem.headline: German churches call for asylum law reform.

text.p: German Roman Catholic and Protestant churches united on Friday to appeal for an urgent reform of the country's asylum laws and a relaxation on citizenship rules for children born to foreigners.

Just weeks after a series of arson attacks on churches in northern Germany, where racists spray-painted swastikas on church walls, church leaders said nations needed to fight the causes of migration rather than the refugees themselves.
They urged lawmakers to set up a more transparent framework for granting citizenship to foreigners and said the number of refugees migrating to Europe and Germany would keep increasing.

"In Germany, we need to improve the social and cultural conditions for integrating foreigners and to counter the reservations and fears caused by xenophobia and racism," said Karl Lehmann, chairman of the German Bishops' Conference.

The churches said it was time to recognise more than people born in Germany had a right to German citizenship. Germany is the only major Western industrial nation to maintain the principle that nationality is determined by blood lines.
The current rules mean eastern Europeans of German descent can find it easier to get a German passport than children of Turkish immigrants who have spent their entire lives here.

Lehmann and Klaus Engelhardt, chairman of the Protestant Church Council in Germany, also said that "church asylum" had to be respected. Under the controversial practice, asylum seekers facing deportation are given shelter in the churches.
But Justice Minister Edzard Schmidt-Jortzig said churches could not be permitted to operate outside the legal system.
"I even think the word asylum in this context is wrong," he told the Leipziger Volkszeitung daily. "Churches can and must not be allowed to create an area outside the law of the state."
At a fire in the northern town of Luebeck last week investigators found Nazi swasktikas sprayed on the walls of the building and a slogan threatening local priest Guenter Harig.
Harig is a well-known campaigner for the rights of asylum-seekers and his parish is currently sheltering an Algerian family under "church asylum".
The churchman's name was also found daubed at the scene of an attack in Luebeck last month, which destroyed a Roman Catholic church.
On June 4, a Protestant church in Hamburg was set on fire after being daubed with right-wing and satanic symbols but the building was only slightly damaged.
